For example,IMareincreasinglyemployedinheating,ventilation,andairconditioning(HVAC) systems, elevators, and other building services that require efficient power management. Integration into building management systems is vital to optimizing energy use, minimizing operational costs, and improving overall building performance. This integration not only contributes to energy efficiency but also plays a role in the comfort and safety of building occupants. This reliance on IM within the building sector is a crucial step towards their strategic role in the larger context of grid-interactive applications. The concept of integration building-to- grid (B2G) represents a transformative approach to energy management, allowing buildings to change from passive energy consumers to dynamic and interactive energy grid compo- nents. ThecomplexityanddynamicnatureofB2Gsystemsrequireaccurateandefficientmodeling of IM. Modeling is crucial as it enables the prediction and optimization of machine perfor- mance in dynamic scenarios, ensuring that systems can efficiently respond to varying de- mandsfrombothbuildingsandthegrid. Acomprehensivemodelalsoimprovesunderstand- ing of the complex interactions between machines, building systems, and the grid, facilitat- ing the development of energy-efficient and sustainable strategies. Additionally, modeling allowssimulationofscenarios,supportinginformeddecision-makinginbuildingdesignand grid integration. Developing a model that accurately represents the complex dynamics of IM in B2G systems presents several challenges. B2G applications care about variables such as terminal voltage, current, PF, and power consumption. The building and energy industry practice requires fast computing speed, such as completing an annual simulation within a fewminutes. Several existing models provide steady or quasi-transient state analysis that considers the operating conditions and responses to resemble steady state to avoid using complex calcu- lations [27]. However, this steady-state assumption is only suitable for mechanical devices, such as chillers and cooling towers, which have response times of minutes to hours. The slow response time is not valid for electrical equipment such as electric motors.
